title: prefill-decode-pipeline-design-stream-priorities-v2
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures the current thinking for the Prefill vs Decode pipeline separation and overlap, with a focus on micro-batching, stream priorities, KV cache consistency, and kernel scheduling. It is a working draft intended to collect trade-offs and an implementation plan for the serving runtime team.

Summary (tl;dr):
- Keep separate logical pipelines for prefill (full-sequence attention / KV population) and decode (autoregressive token generation), but allow controlled overlap to improve GPU utilization and reduce end-to-end latency for short requests.
- Introduce a micro-batching scheduler that understands request phase (PREFILL vs DECODE), stream priority (interactive vs background), and kernel cost estimates; scheduler will form micro-batches within a bounded latency window and optionally co-locate small decode steps with prefill micro-batches when safe.
- KV cache must be versioned per-request and support fast copy-on-write semantics across overlapped execution; prefer small per-GPU metadata to avoid host-GPU round trips.
- Prioritize deterministic fallbacks: if overlap would violate latency SLOs or KV consistency, fall back to strict pipeline separation.

Background and motivation:
- Prefill: handles the initial forward pass over the prompt (long context) to populate KV cache. Often expensive (long sequence attention) and latency-dominant for long prompts.
- Decode: iterative autoregressive generation using KV cache; frequent small kernel launches and many small GPU executions.
- Historically we ran prefill and decode separately (prefill first, then decode loop). This yields predictable semantics and simple KV ownership, but underutilizes GPUs for short requests or when many small decode steps could be fused.
- Overlap idea: begin executing the first decode steps of short/interactive requests while later segments of a prefill for other requests are still finishing. Potential win for tail latency and throughput, but introduces complexity in scheduling, KV cache correctness, and kernel selection.

Design goals and constraints:
- Correctness: output must match non-overlapped results for pinned model versions (modulo allowed non-determinism from lower precision kernels).
- Latency SLOs: interactive streams have hard latency windows (e.g., 100-300ms per token) and should be prioritized.
- Throughput and GPU utilization: increase utilization by micro-batching and co-locating small decode ops with complementary prefill work.
- Predictability: avoid jitter where a small interactive request suddenly experiences long delays due to large prefill batches.
- Minimal host-GPU synchronization: KV cache ops and copy-on-write must be implemented to avoid extra host synchronizations when possible.

Core components:
1) Phase-aware request metadata
   - Each request carries phase: PREFILL / DECODE / STREAMING_DECODE (for streaming/low-latency flows).
   - Priority label: HIGH (interactive), MEDIUM (standard), LOW (background/batch).
   - Estimated kernel cost hint: approximate FLOPs or token-length-derived cost; used for batch packing heuristics.

2) Micro-batching scheduler (MS)
   - Windowing: scheduler opens short windows (configurable: 5-30ms) to collect requests, grouped by model variant, dtype, and device availability.
   - Phase grouping: prefer to build homogeneous micro-batches (all PREFILL or all DECODE). Allow heterogenous batches only when it increases utilization without violating priority constraints.
   - Stream priorities: enforce a fast-path for HIGH priority requests: either preempt current non-critical micro-batches or always reserve a fraction of GPU slots for HIGH priority low-latency decode steps.
   - Cost-aware packing: use a first-fit decreasing heuristic based on estimated kernel cost to cap per-batch cost under target execution time (e.g., 40ms).

3) Overlap rules (safety net)
   - Condition A (KV safe): Overlap permitted only if the decode request's KV read-set is disjoint from the prefill request's KV write-set, OR if we can apply copy-on-write semantics without expensive device-to-host copies.
   - Condition B (priority): A HIGH priority decode can preempt LOW priority prefill, but we must avoid breaking an in-flight grouped prefill that would suffer from partial execution. Preemption modeled as: we allow insertion of decode micro-batch between prefill micro-batches only at sequence boundaries where attention/kernels allow.
   - Condition C (kernel compatibility): Kernel selection must support mixed-prefill/decode execution (e.g., prefill uses long-attn kernels, decode uses cached-kv kernels). If hardware kernel implementations conflict (e.g., different workspace or cuBLAS streams), scheduler must serialize.

4) KV cache design for overlap
   - Versioned KV pointers: each request keeps a lightweight KV handle with a version id. When overlap requires modifying KV (e.g., prefill writing while another decode reads), we allocate a per-GPU slab for copy-on-write pages; slab allocation is bounded to avoid OOM.
   - Fast-path: common case is decode reads after prefill from the same request - that's trivial. The tricky case is independent requests whose execution overlaps. For those we avoid writes to shared model-global buffers; all KV per-request.
   - GC: retired KV versions reclaimed asynchronously; meta GC triggered by epoch counters and a per-device memory watermark.

5) Kernel selection and launch semantics
   - Kernel registry annotated with: phase (PREFILL/DECODE), expected seq-len range, memory workspace requirement, and whether kernel supports being fused into multi-request micro-batch.
   - When forming mixed micro-batches, scheduler queries kernel registry to ensure a compatible kernel exists; if not, fall back to serial execution.
   - Use CUDA stream pool with priority streams: HIGH priority decode micro-batches use high-priority CUDA streams; scheduler maps micro-batch logical prioritization to stream priority to improve latency.

Trade-offs and open questions:
- Complexity vs benefit: Overlap increases code complexity significantly (KV versioning, preemption, mixed kernel compatibility). We need a data-driven threshold for enabling overlap per model and region.
- Memory pressure: copy-on-write KV slabs will increase memory pressure on GPU; need concrete heuristics to limit and to degrade gracefully (e.g., block overlap when free memory < X%).
- Determinism: different packing heuristics and kernel choices can change model outputs subtly (quantization / kernel non-determinism). Must surface this to customers as an opt-in perf mode.
- Metricization: need fine-grained metrics (per-request latency broken down into queuing / kernel exec / memcpy / kv-copy), plus histogram of micro-batch sizes and overlap frequency.

Implementation plan (phased):
Phase 0 - instrumentation (2 weeks):
  - Add per-request phase metadata and cost hints to current RPC layer.
  - Emit metrics for prefill vs decode times (existing and per-kernel).
Phase 1 - scheduler primitives (4 weeks):
  - Implement micro-batching windows, cost-aware packing, and priority labeling.
  - Ensure pure-PREFILL and pure-DECODE micro-batches work with new scheduler (no overlap yet).
Phase 2 - KV safety and copy-on-write (4-6 weeks):
  - Implement per-request KV handles, device slab allocator, and GC hooks.
  - Tests: stress tests for concurrent KV allocation and reclamation.
Phase 3 - controlled overlap (6-8 weeks):
  - Enable overlap for low-risk scenarios (short decode + long prefill for different requests) behind feature flag.
  - Add kernel registry checks and CUDA stream prioritization mapping.
Phase 4 - rollout and telemetry (ongoing):
  - A/B tests, canary on small fleet, automated rollback triggers if latency regressions or OOMs detected.

Operational considerations:
- Feature flags: overlap disabled by default; enable per-customer/model via runtime config.
- Safety alarms: OOM spike, per-request tail latency increases, or micro-batch exec time variance trigger immediate rollback.
- Developer ergonomics: expose a "deterministic" serving mode that forces strict phase separation and deterministic kernels for customers that require byte-for-byte reproducibility.

TODOs and open action items:
- [ ] Run microbenchmarks for kernel compatibility across our common models (GPT-like, MixTransformer, long-context models) - assigned to Priya (JIRA-SERV-971).
- [ ] Define concrete memory watermark thresholds for KV slab allocation and GC - assigned to Evan.
- [ ] Add telemetry hooks for overlap frequency and time-since-registration for each micro-batch - assigned to Lena.
- [ ] Draft customer-facing doc explaining opt-in perf mode and determinism trade-offs.

References and related docs:
- prefill-vs-decode-pipeline-design.json (prior doc), prefill-decode-pipeline-design-draft.json (earlier draft), prefill-vs-decode-pipeline-microbatching-spec.json
- JIRA: JIRA-SERV-971 (scheduler micro-batching epic)
- GH: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/214 (prototype scheduler change)

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus review on the overlap safety rules and KV copy-on-write approach. Those are the riskiest pieces.
- If we want faster time-to-value, we can start by implementing a HIGH-priority fast-path only (no general overlap), which will still yield tail latency wins for interactive streams with less engineering effort.

Changelog:
- v2 (this doc): added concrete overlap rules, copy-on-write KV plan, phased implementation timeline (2024-10-01 -> 2024-11-12).
